Standard Greek compound; pro- and gnos- are productive roots in English.
Standard Greek compound; dia- and gnos- both productive in English. The -e is part of the root's form in this verb.

Standard Greek compound; tele- and phon- both productive in English.

Standard Greek compound of "life" and "study of".
Two productive Greek roots (bio- appears in biology, biosphere; graph- appears in photograph, grammar) combined with a noun-forming suffix.
Standard Greek compound; anti-, bio-, and -tic are all productive morphemes in English.
Two productive Greek roots (geo- 'earth' and graph- 'write/record') combined with a noun-forming suffix -y. The 'o' in 'geo' serves as the connective vowel.
Standard Greek compound; geo- and -logy both productive in English.
Two productive Greek roots joined by a connective vowel.
Standard Greek prefix + Latin root + Latin suffix. All parts are productive and clearly identifiable.
Standard Greek compound; micro- and scop- both productive in English.
Standard Greek compound; auto- and graph- both productive in English.
Standard Greek compound of 'cardi-' (heart) and '-logy' (study of).
Standard Greek compound of derm- (skin) and -logy (study of), joined by a connective vowel.
Productive Greek roots 'ped-' (child) and 'iatr-' (physician/heal) combined with the common Greek adjectival suffix '-ic'.

Two productive Greek roots (dem- appears in epidemic, endemic; crat- appears in aristocrat, autocrat) joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. Emit -o- as a separate morpheme so both roots are individually visible to the learner.
Two productive Greek roots joined by connective vowel. The -y suffix nominalises the compound.
Productive Greek roots 'phil-' (love) and 'anthrop-' (human) joined by a connective vowel, with a common noun-forming suffix '-y'.

Latin root "dict-" meaning "say/tell" combined with the Latin suffix "-ionary" meaning "place for/collection of".
Standard Latin compound; pre- and dict- both productive in English.

Single-morpheme word. While it contains the Latin root 'mem-', the '-ory' ending is part of the original Latin word 'memoria' and not a separate, productive English suffix in this context.
False-root trap. Not un- + cle; from Latin avunculus, double diminutive of avus (grandfather).

False-root trap. Looks like butt + -er agent suffix but is from Greek boutyron / Latin butyrum. The "-er" is part of the borrowed stem.
Standard Greek compound with two productive roots joined by a connective vowel and a noun-forming suffix.
Compound of two productive Greek roots and a Greek noun-forming suffix. The 'o' in 'xeno' acts as a combining vowel.
Standard Latin compound; omni- and vor- both productive in English.

Standard Latin compound: re- (again) + nov- (new) + -ate (verb-forming suffix). All parts are productive.
